questions.q: How does this lesson's view of alert fatigue differ from the SOC course's coverage of it?
options: This lesson covers alert fatigue only for security alerts, not resource alerts
This lesson claims alert fatigue is not a real problem
There is no difference; both courses cover the exact same angle
This lesson looks at it from the configuration side — where it's created on day one — rather than the analyst side where it's experienced
questions.explain: The SOC course covered the analyst experiencing a flood of alerts; this lesson covers the deployment decisions that create that flood in the first place.

questions.q: Why does setting a CPU alert at 70% instead of 85% "backfire," according to this lesson?
options: Normal daily load can sit at 70-75%, so the alert fires repeatedly for nothing wrong, training people to dismiss it
Azure and AWS don't allow thresholds below 85%
It backfires only on AWS, not on Azure
A 70% threshold uses significantly more compute resources to evaluate
questions.explain: A threshold set below normal operating load fires constantly for non-problems, and repeated false alarms teach people to dismiss alerts generally.

questions.q: What happened to the 85% CPU threshold once it was observed against two weeks of real traffic?
options: It was removed because it provided no useful information
It fired constantly, just like the 70% threshold
It had to be lowered further to catch any problems at all
It never fired on normal load, confirming it was tuned correctly as a real signal rather than noise
questions.explain: A threshold that stays quiet during normal operation and only fires on genuine problems is evidence it's set correctly.

questions.q: What is the "real practice" this lesson recommends for building out an alert set?
options: Use the same alert thresholds on every deployment regardless of its actual traffic
Wait until after a major incident before configuring any alerts
Configure every possible alert immediately so nothing is ever missed
Start with a small, high-confidence set, observe real behavior for a while, then expand deliberately one alert at a time
questions.explain: Expanding the alert set should be a decision made from observed behavior against this specific environment, not a one-time setup checklist.

questions.q: What is the real danger once alert fatigue sets in from a noisy, over-sensitive alert?
options: Only that one specific alert gets ignored, with no effect on any other alert
People start reflexively dismissing alerts in general, including the ones that actually matter
The environment automatically raises its own threshold to compensate
The noisy alert automatically disables itself after enough false positives
questions.explain: Once people learn that alerts here don't reliably mean something is wrong, that habit spreads beyond the one noisy alert.
